sources.title: Export the fixture environment and add the shared test helper
sources.author: faviann
sources.body:
## Parent

#201

## What to build

`./validate.sh` becomes genuinely non-live, rather than claiming to be.

It is documented as deterministic and non-live and is neither. It cannot start without the machine-local vault passphrase, because Ansible decrypts the vault group while loading the tracked inventory — even for a fixture play targeting the local controller. And 34 of its 44 direct-Ansible regression tests inherit that tracked inventory, with fixture plays naming real hosts; the only thing keeping them off the network is a hand-written `connection: local` in each play. "Isolated" is a convention held up by per-fixture discipline, not a property.

Make the boundary a property of the command. `./validate.sh` exports the Ansible inventory and vault-password-file variables, pointing at fixtures inside the test tree, **once for its whole run**. Everything beneath inherits them, including the registered lifecycle launchers. No test file needs an inventory edit for this to take effect.

The guard is structural rather than a promise: the fixture inventory carries no host addresses and no SSH settings, so a fixture play that forgets `connection: local` fails to resolve a name instead of reaching a managed host. Today that same mistake reaches the real host.

Add the **shared test helper** that will replace the duplicated raw playbook literal, and have it assert the fixture environment is in effect — naming the supported command when it is not. The helper takes an explicit "this test supplies its own inventory" declaration, so the eight tests that pass their own inventory opt out by declaration rather than by omission.

This is the **expand** half of a wide refactor. Nothing is migrated here; the helper lands beside the existing literal so nothing breaks. The two migration batches are:

- **Batch A** — the 19 test files registered behind the lifecycle regression runner
- **Batch B** — the 20 standalone regression files collected directly

Measured before designing this: all 34 inventory-inheriting tests were run against a three-host fixture inventory and a dummy passphrase, and **34 of 34 passed unchanged**. Nothing in the regression suite depends on the real inventory or the real vault.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A fixture inventory and fixture passphrase live inside the test tree
- [ ] The fixture inventory carries no host addresses and no SSH settings
- [ ] `./validate.sh` exports both once for its whole run, and everything beneath inherits them
- [ ] `./validate.sh` completes on a machine with no vault passphrase file present
- [ ] A shared test helper exists that constructs the locked playbook invocation and asserts the fixture environment is in effect
- [ ] When the assertion fails, the message names `./validate.sh tests` as the supported path
- [ ] The helper accepts an explicit declaration for tests that supply their own inventory
- [ ] An ADR records enforcing the non-live boundary in the validation command, its rejected alternatives, and its recorded boundaries
- [ ] `./validate.sh` passes

## Out of scope

- Migrating any test file to the helper — that is batches A and B
- The test-literal guard, which lands only once no file writes the literal
- Making the suite offline; the boundary is no managed host, no vault secret, no machine-specific credential, and public-network reads remain permitted

## Blocked by

None — can start immediately.

sources.title: Replace raw uv invocations with six purpose-named Bash commands
sources.author: faviann
sources.body:
Implements the design resolved by [Design stable Bash command interfaces for homelab-iac](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/189). Every decision below traces to a closed ticket on that map; the consolidated matrix is in [#198's resolution](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/198#issuecomment-5418235197).

## Problem Statement

Getting this repository to do anything requires knowing raw `uv` incantations. Tracked guidance teaches 25 distinct raw command shapes across 36 lines in seven files, and the wider tree carries 103 more. There are two Bash commands — `./run.sh` and `./validate.sh` — and they own only two operations between them. Everything else is a raw command copied out of a README.

That costs three different people three different ways.

**An operator** cannot tell which commands are safe. `./run.sh` serializes lifecycle mutation behind a lock; the raw provisioning command printed in `README.md` does the same work with no lock at all. Connectivity, credential, and API diagnostics are three separate raw playbook invocations with overlapping content and no shared vocabulary, and one of them always exits `0` even when a host is unreachable.

**An agent** is told by `AGENTS.md` to run Ansible tools through `uv run --locked <tool>` — and then handed a merged-variable debugging command that prints 73 vault-derived lines. That command is the largest secret-disclosure surface in the tracked guidance, and it is documented as the way to debug. Agents also cannot distinguish an approved raw command from one that happens to appear in a document.

**A contributor** has one feedback command, `./validate.sh`, which runs everything and takes minutes. Every targeted alternative — lint alone, one launcher, one test file — is a raw command they must learn. Worse, `./validate.sh` is described as deterministic and non-live, and it is neither: it cannot start without the machine-local vault passphrase, 34 of its 44 direct-Ansible regression tests inherit the real inventory and are kept off the network only by a hand-written `connection: local` in each fixture, and one unit test decrypts the vault and sends a real bearer token to the live Authentik API on every real workstation.

The through-line: the command surface is an accident of history rather than a designed interface, so safety properties are unenforceable, secrets leak through documented paths, and nobody can tell what they are allowed to run.

## Solution

Six purpose-named Bash commands become the entire supported interface, for contributors, operators, and agents alike.

| Command | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `./setup.sh` | Guided workstation setup, plus targeted controller reconciliation |
| `./vault.sh` | Vault configuration, editing, verification, key transfer, passphrase rotation |
| `./validate.sh` | Comprehensive non-live handoff validation, plus targeted feedback |
| `./inspect.sh` | Read-only managed-host diagnostics and inventory observation |
| `./recover.sh` | Narrow state-restoring recovery |
| `./run.sh` | Full, provision-only, and configure-only lifecycle execution |

Every raw command that gains an owner is **removed** from tracked guidance rather than kept as a compatibility shim — a raw form left in a document is the form the next agent copies. Five raw commands survive as recorded standing permissions, each carrying its trigger, audience, scope, boundary, and escalation condition.

Three properties become true that are only claimed today:

- **`./validate.sh` needs no machine-local secret.** It exports a fixture inventory and fixture passphrase once for its whole run, so the non-live boundary is a property of the command rather than a convention held up by per-fixture discipline.
- **No supported operation prints a secret.** The merged-variable command survives as `./inspect.sh vars` and prints **masked values** — letters as `a`, digits as `9`, every other character literal, whitespace as a visible token — so the fault class this repository actually suffers from stays diagnosable while the secret does not print.
- **Read-only live operations cannot observe state mid-transition.** The lifecycle lock splits into shared and exclusive classes, so a diagnostic takes a shared lock and a lifecycle run takes an exclusive one.

Nine tests reachable from `./validate.sh` enforce the result, and one new document, `docs/command-policy.md`, holds the policy that `AGENTS.md` is too small to carry.

## User Stories

### Discovering and running commands

1. As a contributor, I want six purpose-named commands rather than 25 raw shapes, so that I can find the operation I need without reading a README first.
2. As a contributor, I want every command to answer `--help` with its operations, so that I can discover the interface from the terminal.
3. As a contributor, I want `./run.sh`, `./validate.sh`, and `./setup.sh` to have safe no-argument defaults, so that the common case needs no arguments.
4. As an operator, I want `./vault.sh`, `./inspect.sh`, and `./recover.sh` to require an explicit operation, so that I never trigger a consequential default by typing a bare command.
5. As a contributor, I want every command to reject an unknown operation or option with a distinct exit status, so that a typo fails loudly instead of being silently ignored.
6. As an agent, I want one documented exit convention across all six commands, so that I can branch on the outcome without special-casing each script.
7. As an operator, I want lock contention to return a status distinct from failure, so that "someone else is deploying" and "the deploy failed" are not the same signal to a script.
8. As an operator, I want a command that cannot take its lock to stop immediately and name the holder, so that I never mistake a wait for a hang during a five-to-ten-minute run.

### Lifecycle execution

9. As an operator, I want `./run.sh` to keep running the **full lifecycle** by default, so that the command I already use does not change meaning.
10. As an operator, I want `./run.sh provision` and `./run.sh configure` to run the **provision-only lifecycle** and **configure-only lifecycle**, so that lifecycle slices have first-class names.
11. As an operator, I want `--stack <name>` instead of an `-e` variable override, so that selecting one stack cannot be confused with defeating a guard.
12. As an operator, I want `--include-controller` instead of an `-e` variable override, so that the single most dangerous flag in the repository has a name that says what it does.
13. As an operator, I want `--limit` to keep Ansible's own grammar — groups, patterns, comma lists, `!` exclusion — so that `--limit cap_docker` keeps working and I learn no second syntax.
14. As an operator, I want every other Ansible argument to move behind `--`, so that low-level passthrough is visibly separate from the supported grammar.
15. As an operator, I want passthrough to be unable to change target selection, **lifecycle intent**, the lock, or wrapper enforcement, so that the escape hatch cannot defeat the safety boundary.
16. As an operator, I want `./run.sh --check` to take a shared rather than exclusive lock, so that a dry run does not block a colleague's diagnostic.

### Diagnostics and inspection

17. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh credentials` to walk the Proxmox API credential and permission ladder, so that one command tells me whether my token works and how far it reaches.
18. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh connectivity` to report SSH reachability of the LXCs, so that I can check the fleet without a raw ad-hoc module call.
19. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh connectivity` to exit non-zero when a target is unreachable, so that I can use it from a script — today's playbook always exits `0`.
20. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh containers` to list the LXCs the Proxmox node actually has, so that I can see a VMID conflict with a container no **LXC identity reservation** covers.
21. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh plan` to run **LXC contract compilation**, **fleet preflight**, **LXC observation**, and produce an **LXC lifecycle plan** per target without executing anything, so that I can see every detected problem before committing to a run.
22. As an agent, I want `./inspect.sh vars <host>` to show merged inventory variables with vault-derived values masked, so that I can debug variable precedence without putting a secret in a transcript.
23. As an agent, I want the mask to preserve every non-alphanumeric character and render whitespace visibly, so that I can diagnose a trailing space or an unescaped `$` — the faults this repository actually hits.
24. As a maintainer, I want the mask to collapse case, so that masked output reaching a pull request does not hand an attacker a wordlist hint.
25. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh vars --graph` to show the group membership tree, so that I can read inventory structure without a raw command.
26. As an operator, I want `./inspect.sh vars` to take no lock, so that a running deploy does not make a local inventory read fail.
27. As an operator, I want the read-only inspect operations to take a shared lock, so that they cannot observe managed-host state part-way through a mutation.

### Recovery

28. As an operator, I want `./recover.sh ssh-keys` to perform **manual SSH recovery**, so that restoring access has a named command rather than a raw playbook invocation.
29. As an operator, I want `./recover.sh ssh-keys` to work when unrelated desired state is invalid, so that ADR-0002's independent recovery guarantee survives the new interface.
30. As an operator, I want `./recover.sh ssh-keys` to establish Proxmox host access itself, so that the manual "run the bootstrap tags first" prerequisite disappears.
31. As an operator, I want `./recover.sh` to require an explicit operation and take an exclusive lock, so that a state-changing recovery is never accidental and never concurrent with a lifecycle run.

### Setup and bootstrap

32. As a contributor on a fresh machine, I want `./setup.sh` with no arguments to walk me through workstation setup, so that the guided path is unchanged.
33. As an agent in a fresh worktree, I want `./setup.sh sync` to materialize the locked controller environment non-interactively, so that I do not run interactive credential onboarding to get three install steps.
34. As an agent in a fresh worktree, I want `./setup.sh bootstrap` to reconcile collections, roles, and the controller SSH key non-interactively, so that a new worktree reaches a runnable state with one documented command.
35. As a contributor, I want `./setup.sh bootstrap` to create the controller SSH key only when absent, so that it never rotates a key the fleet already trusts.
36. As a contributor, I want `./setup.sh sync` and `bootstrap` to remain independent repair paths, so that I can fix one layer without re-running the other.
37. As a contributor, I want guided setup to leave an existing encrypted vault untouched, so that re-running setup is never destructive.

### Vault

38. As an operator, I want `./vault.sh configure` to prompt through a TTY for Proxmox credentials, so that secrets never pass through arguments or environment variables.
39. As an operator, I want reconfiguration to preserve every unrelated vault key, so that updating credentials cannot silently drop another stack's secret.
40. As an operator, I want `./vault.sh edit` to open the whole encrypted vault in my editor, so that general editing has one obvious path.
41. As an agent, I want `./vault.sh check` to verify the vault non-disclosingly — header, passphrase file existence and permissions, decryptability, structure, required keys present and non-placeholder — so that I can confirm the vault is sound without seeing a value.
42. As an agent, I want `./vault.sh set <key> --from-file <path>` to move a secret into the vault without reading it, so that I can perform a requested credential transfer without the secret entering my transcript.
43. As an operator, I want `--create` and `--replace` to be explicit and mutually exclusive, so that a transfer cannot silently overwrite or silently create.
44. As an operator, I want the source file for a transfer to be rejected unless it is a current-user-owned regular file with no group or world permissions, so that a transfer cannot pick up a world-readable or symlinked secret.
45. As an operator, I want `./vault.sh rotate` to keep its confirmation, tmpfs handling, rekey-before-publish ordering, ciphertext backup, verification, and rollback behaviour, so that passphrase rotation loses none of its existing safety.
46. As an agent, I want `./vault.sh rotate --dry-run` to rehearse on throwaway copies, so that I can verify rotation logic without touching the real vault, Bitwarden, or the live passphrase.
47. As an operator, I want no supported operation that prints decrypted vault contents, so that the disclosure path documented today simply ceases to exist.
48. As an operator, I want vault plaintext to exist only in a mode-700 tmpfs workspace and never at the tracked vault path, so that an interrupted operation cannot leave plaintext on disk.
49. As an operator, I want a failed vault mutation to leave the original file untouched, so that a partial write cannot corrupt the vault.

### Targeted feedback

50. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh` with no arguments to remain the comprehensive handoff command, so that the required pre-handoff step does not change.
51. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh lint` for repo-wide lint alone, so that I get fast style feedback while iterating.
52. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh lifecycle` for the fast lifecycle regression path, so that I get lifecycle feedback in about a minute and a half instead of six.
53. As a contributor, I want `--full`, `--only <launcher.py>` (repeatable), and `--fail-fast` on that operation, so that every selection mode the runner already supports has a supported command form.
54. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh tests [<target>…]` to select test files or node ids, so that I can iterate on one test without learning a raw invocation.
55. As a contributor, I want test targets outside the test tree rejected as invalid usage, so that the operation cannot become a general test runner.
56. As a stack maintainer, I want `./validate.sh stack <path>` to validate one **stack update policy**, so that per-stack policy checking has a supported command.
57. As a developer integrating with stack tooling, I want `./validate.sh stack` to emit schema-versioned JSON on stdout with diagnostics on stderr, so that later image-update planning can consume it as a stable contract.
58. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh stack` excluded from the no-argument handoff run, so that handoff does not depend on every upstream vendor repository being reachable.
59. As a contributor, I want a targeted operation to never substitute for the full handoff run, so that the required verification path stays unambiguous.

### The non-live boundary

60. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh` to need no machine-local vault passphrase, so that validation runs on a machine that was never manually configured.
61. As a contributor, I want `./validate.sh` to export a fixture inventory once for its whole run, so that no regression test can inherit the real inventory.
62. As a contributor, I want the fixture inventory to carry no host addresses or SSH settings, so that a fixture play missing `connection: local` fails to resolve a name instead of reaching a managed host.
63. As a contributor, I want one shared test helper instead of 39 copies of a raw playbook literal, so that changing how tests invoke Ansible is one edit.
64. As a contributor, I want the helper to assert the fixture environment is in effect and name the supported command when it is not, so that a test run outside `./validate.sh` fails loudly rather than running live.
65. As a contributor, I want the eight tests that supply their own inventory to opt out by declaration, so that the exceptions are enumerable in one place rather than invisible by omission.
66. As a maintainer, I want the non-live boundary stated as *no managed host, no vault secret, no machine-specific credential* rather than "offline", so that the promise matches what the suite actually does — public-network reads included.
67. As a maintainer, I want the only test that sends a live credential to a managed host deleted along with the code path it exercised, so that the test suite stops authenticating against the production Authentik API.

### Safety for agents

68. As a maintainer, I want `AGENTS.md` to instruct agents to use the Bash commands and not to invoke Ansible, `uv`, or `pytest` directly, so that the instruction stops contradicting the design.
69. As a maintainer, I want a human-approved raw command to not be automatically agent-safe, so that permission for a person is never silently inherited by an agent.
70. As a maintainer, I want silence to mean human-only, so that an agent cannot infer permission from the absence of a prohibition.
71. As an agent, I want read-only SSH diagnosis of a named host to be a recorded standing permission, so that I can investigate a live problem without asking for each observation.
72. As a maintainer, I want that permission to forbid reading or printing secrets and forbid any mutation, so that diagnosis cannot become an unreviewed change.
73. As a maintainer, I want the masked-value exemption scoped to one command with one documented mask, so that it is not a general licence for an agent to invent its own masking.
74. As an agent, I want each surviving raw command to carry its trigger, audience, scope, boundary, sensitive-output constraint, and escalation condition, so that I can tell an approved exception from an accident of documentation.

### Enforcement

75. As a maintainer, I want the command grammar and exit conventions covered by tests, so that the contract cannot drift silently.
76. As a maintainer, I want lock class per operation covered by tests, so that a refactor cannot quietly turn a shared lock exclusive or an exclusive lock shared.
77. As a maintainer, I want the check-mode audit pinned as a snapshot, so that a future task that writes in check mode fails a test instead of silently making the shared lock wrong.
78. As a maintainer, I want live-playbook coverage derived rather than hand-listed, so that the next live playbook someone adds is caught without anyone remembering to update a list.
79. As a maintainer, I want tracked text checked for superseded commands and option forms, so that a document cannot keep teaching the form the migration removed.
80. As a maintainer, I want text that a script *prints* included in that check, so that a message arriving at the moment of failure — the most-copied guidance in the repository — cannot teach a dead command.
81. As a maintainer, I want prose that quotes a superseded form in order to warn against it to be allowlisted, so that correct guidance does not fail the check that protects it.
82. As a maintainer, I want the allowlist to be the exception record itself, so that the two cannot drift apart.
83. As a maintainer, I want a guard against a new test copying the raw playbook literal, so that the shared helper does not decay back into per-file discipline.
84. As a maintainer, I want the mask covered both as a pure function and end-to-end against a fixture vault, so that a disclosure is a test failure rather than a discovery.
85. As a maintainer, I want every agent-permitted vault operation asserted to disclose no fixture secret, so that "no operation prints vault contents" is enforced rather than assumed.

### Migration

86. As a contributor, I want every stack README's deploy line to use `--stack`, so that copying a neighbouring README does not propagate the removed form.
87. As an operator, I want the workstation persistent-state runbook migrated to the named options, so that the document `AGENTS.md` requires me to read does not teach the flag the migration removed.
88. As a contributor, I want the legacy vault scripts deleted outright rather than shimmed, so that there is one obvious path and nothing to remove later.
89. As an operator, I want the playbooks behind the new operations to remain as playbooks, so that only their entry points change and their behaviour is reviewable.
90. As an agent, I want `docs/command-policy.md` to hold the vocabulary, permissions, allowlist, and recorded boundaries, so that `AGENTS.md` stays short enough to read in full every session.
91. As a maintainer, I want each ADR to land with the change it describes, so that the reasoning is findable beside the code rather than in a closed issue.

## Implementation Decisions

### Command vocabulary and grammar

Six purpose-named top-level scripts, no generic dispatcher, no separate raw interface for agents. Invocation is `./command.sh [operation] [supported options] [-- low-level arguments]`.

A seventh command is justified only by a distinct safety boundary, availability requirement, or operator purpose; related operations stay together as operations or options.

Exit status across all six: `0` success, `1` failed check or operation, `2` invalid usage, `75` another holder has the lock. `75` is returned only by `./run.sh`, `./inspect.sh`, and `./recover.sh`.

Only `./run.sh` accepts low-level passthrough, and only after `--`. Passthrough cannot change target selection, **lifecycle intent**, the lock, or wrapper enforcement.

Stable behaviour comprises documented names, operations, options, exit behaviour, safety guarantees, and any explicit output format. Ordinary terminal prose is human-facing and is not a machine interface. `./validate.sh stack`'s schema-versioned JSON is the only machine interface in the repository, justified by a concrete downstream consumer.

Full operation table, with lock class, prerequisite layers, and agent-safety:

| Command | Operation | Lock | Layers | Agent-safe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | :---: |
| `./setup.sh` | *(default)* guided setup | — | — | no |
| | `sync` | — | — | yes |
| | `bootstrap` | — | — | yes |
| `./vault.sh` | `configure` | — | — | no |
| | `edit` | — | — | no |
| | `check` | — | — | yes |
| | `set <key> --from-file <path> --create\|--replace [--strip-final-newline]` | — | — | on explicit request |
| | `rotate` | — | — | no |
| | `rotate --dry-run` | — | — | yes |
| `./validate.sh` | *(default)* comprehensive handoff | — | — | yes |
| | `lint` | — | — | yes |
| | `lifecycle [--full] [--only <launcher.py>]… [--fail-fast]` | — | — | yes |
| | `tests [<target>…]` | — | — | yes |
| | `stack <path>` | — | — | yes |
| `./inspect.sh` | `credentials` | shared | L1 | yes |
| | `connectivity [--limit <targets>]` | shared | L1 | yes |
| | `containers` | shared | L1 | yes |
| | `plan [--limit <targets>]` | shared | L1 + L3 | yes |
| | `vars <host>` / `vars --graph` | none | — | yes |
| `./recover.sh` | `ssh-keys [--limit <targets>]` | exclusive | L1 + L3 | no |
| `./run.sh` | *(default)* **full lifecycle** | exclusive | L1 + L3 | yes |
| | `provision` — **provision-only lifecycle** | exclusive | L1 + L3 | yes |
| | `configure` — **configure-only lifecycle** | exclusive | L1 + L3 | yes |
| | `--check` on any form | shared | L1 + L3 | yes |

`./run.sh` first-class options: `--limit <targets>` (Ansible's grammar unchanged), `--check`, `--stack <name>`, `--include-controller`, `-v`/`-vv`/`-vvv`.

### The live-execution library

One Bash library file, read with `source` by `./run.sh`, `./inspect.sh`, and `./recover.sh`. It owns live execution only: lock acquisition and lock class, wrapper marker export, prerequisite-layer selection, and the locked playbook call. Argument parsing, `--help`, and exit codes stay per command — the six grammars genuinely differ, and a shared parser for six differing grammars is a framework for six callers.

A hidden `./run.sh` subcommand was rejected: it is a real argv surface pretending not to be one, and the grammar rule requires every command to validate its arguments and reject unknown input.

The non-live commands (`./validate.sh`, `./vault.sh`, `./setup.sh`) call `uv run --locked <tool>` directly. `uv run --locked` already materializes the locked environment, so there is no shared setup step to factor out — only a three-token prefix.

**The internal-call rule**, replacing any maintained list: *a script may call `uv run --locked <tool>` directly if and only if that call contacts no managed host. Anything that contacts a managed host goes through the live library.*

### The lock model

Lock class follows the operation class, not the command. Read-only live operations take a **shared** lock; mutating operations take an **exclusive** lock; operations contacting no managed host take none.

A command that cannot take its lock stops immediately, naming the holder from the pid and worktree the lock file already records. No `--wait` option: a lifecycle run lasts five to ten minutes, so waiting is indistinguishable from hanging, and "a lifecycle run is in progress" is frequently the answer the operator needs.

`./run.sh --check` taking a shared lock rests on an audit, not an assumption: fifteen tasks carry `check_mode: false` and every one is a read probe; the repository's one custom module declares check-mode support and branches on it; no task uses the one module that ignores check mode.

The lock remains **machine-local**. Its scope must stay explicit wherever it is documented.

### Prerequisite layers

The current prerequisite playbook mixes concerns and breaks ADR-0002, because **manual SSH recovery** must not be blocked by an unrelated host's invalid desired state. It splits into two importable layers:

- **L1 — control node health**: wrapper marker assertion, virtualenv presence, collection version match. Every live playbook imports it.
- **L3 — Proxmox host access**: SSH access setup and validation. Imported only by operations that need it.

The cross-LXC `default_domain` assertion moves into **fleet preflight** as a problem record, where the other cross-LXC invariants live and where problems are collected and reported together rather than stopping at the first. It is therefore **not a selectable layer** — it is a property of the playbooks that run fleet preflight. Scripts declare two layers, not three, and no L2 artifact exists to create.

Consequence: `./recover.sh ssh-keys` gets L1 and L3 and never runs fleet preflight, so recovery survives invalid unrelated desired state. It keeps ADR-0002's minimal identity validation — vmid, hostname, resolved control-node public key — with no **LXC contract compilation**.

### Masked-value inspection

`./inspect.sh vars` masks vault-derived values by character class rather than redacting them:

- every letter becomes `a`; every digit becomes `9`
- every other character stays visible exactly as it is
- whitespace renders as a visible token (space, newline, tab)
- a run of more than 16 identical mask characters collapses to a count
- case is **not** preserved

So `Summer$2024` shows as `aaaaaa$9999`.

Redaction to a fixed string was rejected because it hides the fault class this repository demonstrably suffers from — the tree carries two independent mitigations for one shell-interpolation bug, which is what a team does after a fault recurs. A closed list of condition flags cannot surface a fault nobody has found yet. Case is collapsed because a preserved case pattern is a wordlist hint, and no fault is diagnosable from case alone.

**Detection**, two rules together:

1. **By name** — the variable is a vault key. Masked with no exceptions list, so non-secret vault keys are masked too; an exceptions list is a list to maintain and to get wrong.
2. **By content** — the value contains a vault value of **8 characters or more**. Masked whole, which catches derived values such as a bearer header that rule 1 misses.

The 8-character threshold is required because the vault holds values like `"true"` and `"587"`; without it, rule 2 masks every variable containing the word "true".

**The vault key/value set is derived from the merged-variable output itself** — every variable named `vault_*` is a vault key and its value is a vault value. The vault group applies to every host, so all keys are already present in that output, which is exactly why it leaks today. This avoids a second whole-vault decryption and keeps the operation to one mask pass over an existing command's output. Consequently the `vault_` prefix becomes a stated contract in the vault example file rather than a convention.

**The mask is a Python module** that the command pipes inventory output through — not inline shell — so its rules are directly testable.

**Scope tripwire**: the operation is one pure mask function plus one pass over an existing command's output. If the implementation needs more than that, remove the operation rather than grow it; the other four inspect operations do not depend on it.

**No reveal mode.** Editing the vault already shows a person every value at a terminal, and `./inspect.sh credentials` tests the token against the API, which is stronger evidence than a value read by eye.

### The non-live boundary

`./validate.sh` exports the Ansible inventory and vault-password-file variables, pointing at fixtures inside the test tree, **once for its whole run**. Everything beneath inherits them, including the registered lifecycle launchers. No test file needs an inventory edit.

The guard is structural rather than a promise: the fixture inventory carries no host addresses and no SSH settings, so a fixture play that omits `connection: local` fails to resolve a name instead of reaching a managed host. Today that same mistake reaches the real host.

A **shared test helper** replaces the 39 duplicated raw playbook literals and asserts the fixture environment is in effect, naming the supported command when it is not. The eight tests that supply their own inventory use the helper and skip that assertion **by declaration**, keeping the exceptions enumerable.

Measured cost of the repair: all 34 inventory-inheriting tests were run against a three-host fixture inventory and a dummy passphrase, and **34 of 34 passed unchanged**. Nothing in the regression suite depends on the real inventory or the real vault.

The boundary is *no managed host, no vault secret, no machine-specific credential*. It is explicitly **not** an offline promise — the suite crosses a real pinned Renovate boundary and per-stack validation clones an upstream repository for a **vendor-tracked stack**.

**The live-credential path is deleted**: the vault-token helper and the from-vault client constructor are removed, the token-file option becomes required, and the integration test class that was its only caller is deleted. The role already passes a token file under `no_log`. This removes the repository's only script-internal whole-vault decryption and the only live-credential path in the test suite, and it is less code than any alternative.

### Bypass prevention

The lifecycle wrapper marker stays exactly as it is — an honest guard-rail against accident, not a security control. The lock class is deliberately **not** encoded in it: the script that sets the marker is the script that took the lock, so a second value adds only a second thing that can be false while the lock is not held.

The marker assertion moves into L1, so every live playbook inherits it rather than only the two that import the prerequisite file today.

**Liveness is derived, not listed**: a playbook is live when any play targets other than the local controller, **or the playbook imports the L3 Proxmox-host play**. The second clause is required — the Proxmox-host play targets the controller locally and is nonetheless live, because it delegates commands over SSH. A survey of all 80 delegations found this to be the only case the first clause misses. Recorded boundary: a future controller-only playbook that delegates to the Proxmox host without importing L3 goes undetected, which is acceptable because L3 is what establishes that access.

### Raw-command governance

Supported commands are the default interface. A raw command may be documented for a human only when it serves a bounded purpose no supported operation owns.

Agent use is a **separate** decision. Guidance must explicitly permit agent use and state trigger, scope, and boundary; silence means human-only, and an agent cannot approve its own exception.

A true live bypass requires explicit human approval for the exact operation and scope; read-only intent alone does not waive it. Conversation-scoped approval covers a one-off operation and expires with the task. A standing permission must be recorded with triggering request, audience, target scope, observational-or-mutating boundary, sensitive-output constraint, and escalation condition.

**Five standing permissions survive**: read-only SSH diagnosis of a named host; the Proxmox-host manual key-injection procedure (human-only, last resort, the only path when the control node itself is broken); the stack-rename remote mutation (with an added no-active-lock precondition); the Proxmox RAM report support script; and the **Renovate adapter** (maintainer-only, because it consumes an **image update scan request** that no in-repo code produces yet, so a wrapper would wrap a caller that does not exist).

The agent path to the adapter's boundary is its contract test via `./validate.sh tests`.

### Superseded forms

Enforced as a rule rather than a list: **in a documented `./run.sh` invocation, `-e` and `--tags` may appear only after `--`.** A list catches the variables someone remembered; the rule catches the next one.

Replacement guidance:

| Superseded form | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| `-e stack_filter=<stack>` | `--stack <stack>` |
| `-e proxmox_skip_self=false` | `--include-controller` |
| `--tags validation` | `./inspect.sh plan` |
| `--tags provision` | `./run.sh provision` |
| `--tags bootstrap` | removed — `./recover.sh ssh-keys` includes L3 |
| any other `-e <var>=<value>` | `-- -e <var>=<value>` |

### Consolidations and deletions

- The connectivity playbook's Proxmox API play is deleted as a duplicate of `credentials`.
- The API check playbook's node-status and container-count checks are already inside `credentials`; only its full container list survives, as `containers`.
- The standalone-validation tags are removed from the site orchestrator; `./inspect.sh plan` replaces them.
- The two legacy vault scripts are deleted outright, with no deprecating shim. This is a single-operator repository with no external consumers; a shim protects nobody and becomes a second thing to remove.
- The playbooks behind the new operations **remain** as playbooks — the scripts invoke them — and only their header comments change.
- Removed with no replacement: the controller dependency import probe and the collection-list diagnostic (both answered better by re-running the idempotent reconciliation that repairs what they only report), the full inventory dump, and the vault view operation.

### Documentation

**`docs/command-policy.md`** is new, linked from `AGENTS.md` and `README.md`. It carries the vocabulary and grammar, the rule for a seventh command, the internal-call rule, the five standing-permission records, the text-check allowlist, the machine-local scope of the lock, the fact that a build server is now possible, and every recorded boundary.

`AGENTS.md` is read in full every session, so it keeps a rewritten command table and its long-running-output discipline, and its non-negotiable becomes: *use the repository's Bash commands; do not invoke Ansible, `uv`, or `pytest` directly; `docs/command-policy.md` gives the approved exceptions.* The weaker "prefer Bash commands, raw is allowed when nothing covers it" form was rejected — it restates the situation that produced this work and hands the agent a judgement it cannot make alone.

**Migration surface: 23 files.** Eleven identified during design, twelve more found by sweeping the tree for the superseded forms — nine stack READMEs, three further sites in the beets-flask stack README, the workstation persistent-state runbook, the roles requirements comment, and one prose warning that quotes the removed form. Runtime and comment text is in scope, because a message printed at the moment of failure is the most-copied guidance in the repository.

### Implementation order

Eight changes.

1. **Delete the live credential path.** No dependencies, and urgent: the integration test class skips on a hardcoded home-directory path, so no later fixture export ever disarms it — until this lands it authenticates against the production Authentik API on every real workstation. Land first.
2. **Prerequisite layers.** Split L1 and L3, relocate the `default_domain` assertion into fleet preflight, rewrite the two remediation messages, update importers. Precedes every script that declares layers.
3. **The live library and the three live commands.** Library, `./run.sh` grammar, `./inspect.sh` and `./recover.sh` created, standalone-validation tags removed, duplicate API play deleted. **ADR: the lock split.**
4. **The non-live boundary.** Fixture inventory and passphrase, the exports, the shared helper, the 39 literal migrations, the eight opt-out declarations. Helper and migrations are one change — the suite is broken in between. **ADR: enforcing the boundary in the validation command.**
5. **`./validate.sh` operations.** `lint`, `lifecycle`, `tests`, `stack`; the existing exact-argv pinning is rewritten into grammar coverage.
6. **`./vault.sh` and `./setup.sh`.** New vault command, legacy scripts deleted, `sync` and `bootstrap` added, echoed follow-ups rewritten.
7. **`./inspect.sh vars` and the mask.** Mask module, `vault_*` derivation, `--graph`. **ADR: the masked value.**
8. **Documentation and text migration.** All 23 files, runtime and comment text, `docs/command-policy.md`, the `AGENTS.md` non-negotiable. Last, because the text check fails until every command it names exists.

### ADRs

Three, each landing with its change: **the masked value** (an agent may print a derivative of a secret; argued both ways; hard to reverse once masked output reaches transcripts); **enforcing the non-live boundary in the validation command** (a validation command silently overrides Ansible's inventory and vault password, and nothing in the test files shows it); and **the shared/exclusive lock split** (surprising that a read-only command locks at all; a real trade-off; amends ADR-0001's linear-execution model and should be findable beside it).

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts **external behaviour** — what a caller observes — not how a script is built internally. The existing exact-argv pinning of the validation command is the anti-pattern to retire: with six commands and roughly twenty operations, that style produces twenty tests that fail on every internal refactor and prove nothing about the contract. The grammar and the exit convention are the stable contract; the argv a script assembles is an implementation detail.

The one exception is live-operation safety, where the argv **is** the guarantee — whether `--stack` and `--include-controller` reach Ansible correctly, and whether passthrough can alter target selection or **lifecycle intent**, is only observable in what the script hands to the playbook.

**Three seams, two of which already exist.**

**Seam 1 — command execution with a stubbed `uv`.** Run the real script with a fake `uv` earlier on `PATH` that captures argv, environment, and the wrapper marker. Prior art: the existing validation-command regression and the lifecycle run-lock regression both do exactly this, the latter also driving lock contention with a sleeping stub and a second process. This seam carries:

- **Grammar contract** — `--help` exits `0` and names the operations; unknown operation and unknown option each exit `2`; the three commands with defaults have them; the three that require an operation exit `2` without one; lock contention exits `75`.
- **Live-operation safety** — lock class per operation, option translation, passthrough containment.
- **Vault non-disclosure** — every agent-permitted vault operation against a fixture vault, asserting no fixture secret in stdout or stderr.
- **Masked-value end-to-end** — the inspect operation against a fixture vault, asserting no fixture secret appears in its output.

**Seam 2 — static analysis over tracked files.** Parse the tree and assert a property. Prior art: the existing stack-policy snapshot test establishes the pinned-snapshot pattern. This seam carries:

- **Check-mode snapshot** — the fifteen `check_mode: false` tasks pinned by file and task name, plus the custom module's declared check-mode support. A new such task fails the test until someone adds it deliberately. An allowlist of read-only modules was rejected: eight of the fifteen use modules that can also write, so the allowlist would have to admit them and would prove nothing.
- **Derived live-playbook coverage** — every live playbook imports L1, with liveness derived by the two-clause rule and one named exception.
- **Guidance text check** — no superseded raw command in tracked text outside the allowlist, and the `-e`/`--tags`-after-`--` rule. Scope: tracked Markdown outside the test tree, the vault example file, the lint config, YAML comment and message text under the playbook tree and site orchestrator, and string literals inside `echo`/`printf` in tracked shell scripts. Shell *execution* lines are excluded — governed instead by the internal-call rule with the derived live-playbook test as its enforcement. The seam is clean: this test covers text that teaches, that rule covers text that executes.
- **Test-literal guard** — no file in the test tree writes the raw playbook literal instead of importing the shared helper. This exists because the boundary repair's claim is "one mechanism, not 34 edits"; without it that claim decays back into the per-file discipline that already failed silently. A test written by copying an old one fails on the guard, and the failure names the helper — the one moment the author is looking for it.

**Seam 3 — the mask as an importable pure function.** New, and the reason the mask is a Python module rather than inline shell. It carries the character-class rules, case collapse, whitespace tokens, run collapse, the 8-character content threshold, and the assertion that every key in the vault example file carries the `vault_` prefix that rule 1 depends on.

**Not a product seam**: the shared test helper is itself the replacement seam for the 39 duplicated literals, and takes an explicit "this test supplies its own inventory" declaration.

**Scoping.** The text-check allowlist is keyed by **file and shape**, not as a global list of permitted strings, and it *is* the exception record made executable — one artifact rather than two that drift. A raw command no permission record covers has no file it is allowed to appear in. Scoping to specific removed shapes rather than any occurrence of a tool name is deliberate, so that prose explaining why something was removed does not trip the check; the four documents that must quote a removed form to forbid it are allowlisted explicitly.

**Recorded boundary on the whole enforcement set**: these guards catch a contributor or agent who ran validation. `AGENTS.md` requires that before handoff, so they cover the documented workflow and nothing beyond it — the same posture as the wrapper marker: an honest guard-rail against accident, not a control.

## Out of Scope

- **Continuous integration.** Now possible for the first time — once validation needs no machine-local secret, a job reduces to check out, install `uv`, run validation — but building it inside this migration mixes two changes and makes a large migration harder to review. Tracked as #200.
- **Cross-control-node locking.** The lock stays machine-local; #174 records the limitation deliberately. This work must keep that scope explicit wherever the lock is documented, because a guard that covers one machine and silently does not cover another is the false-confidence failure mode.
- **The beets-flask SSH runbook.** Its commands operate on media-library data inside a container that Ansible holds no desired state for, so it is a stack runbook rather than the controller command interface. Its read-only forms already fall under the SSH diagnosis permission; its two mutating ones require a person.
- **An offline guarantee for the workstation regressions.** #175 stays open. The fixture environment makes the suite *non-live*, not *offline*; three workstation fixtures still reach a public host when their overrides are dropped. Nothing here should be read as satisfying it.
- **Redesigning Ansible-native LXC lifecycle policy.** Unchanged.
- **Weakening lock or wrapper enforcement**, and **making validation contact managed hosts**. Both are ruled out.
- **Structured output for anything but per-stack validation.** A machine format is added only for a concrete consumer, and no other exists.
- **A reveal mode for masked values.** Deliberately absent.

## Further Notes

**#169 is answered by this work.** `./setup.sh sync` and `./setup.sh bootstrap` are the non-interactive, idempotent fresh-worktree entry point it asks for; it should close with change 6, with its worktree facts folded into the `AGENTS.md` edit in change 8.

**The `AGENTS.md` non-negotiable becomes actively wrong the moment this lands**, since it currently instructs agents to do the thing this removes. That edit is not cosmetic and belongs with the rest of change 8.

**Two prior corrections are already recorded** on the map's closed tickets and are folded into the decisions above: the inspect `vars` operation takes no prerequisite layer at all (it reads local inventory files and runs no playbook), and the check-mode audit's original claim that no custom module directory exists is false — the conclusion survives because that module declares check-mode support, but the test should assert the module directly rather than rest on the absence of a directory.

**Nothing in `.agents/skills/create-stack/` changes** — re-audited, it contains no tool or script invocation.

**The domain glossary and `CLAUDE.md` are unchanged.** Every term introduced by this work describes the command interface, not the infrastructure lifecycle, so none belongs in the glossary.

**Sizing.** Change 4 is the largest single change (39 test-file migrations behind one mechanism) and change 8 touches the most files (23 documents plus runtime text), but neither contains an unresolved decision. Changes 1 and 2 are small and unblock everything else.

sources.title: Design stable Bash command interfaces for homelab-iac
sources.author: faviann
sources.body:
## Destination

An implementation-ready command-interface design that gives every tracked contributor-, operator-, and agent-facing raw `uv` invocation exactly one disposition: a supported top-level Bash command, an explicitly permitted low-level raw command, or removal. The resolved design must define the command vocabulary, exact responsibility and safety boundaries, targeted feedback paths, enforcement, and migration well enough to pass through `/to-spec` and `/to-tickets` without further architectural decisions.

## Notes

This is a planning-only map. Do not implement production changes while resolving it.

Use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` for every decision ticket. Start each session from the current tracked repository state and use the lifecycle terms in `CONTEXT.md`.

Fixed premises:

- `./validate.sh` remains the comprehensive, deterministic, non-live handoff command.
- `./run.sh` remains the exclusive serialized command for normal operations that contact managed hosts, including check mode; preserve its lock and lifecycle-wrapper enforcement.
- Audit all tracked guidance, scripts, and tests. Direct tool calls in isolated tests may remain only when they cannot contact managed hosts. Script-internal `uv` calls are part of the architecture audit even when they are not public commands.
- Approved exceptional and one-off operations remain possible. Prefer routing live exceptions through `./run.sh`; any true bypass needs explicit approval, exact scope, safety rules, and an agent-use decision. Require an ADR only when the choice is hard to reverse, surprising, and based on a real trade-off.
- Keep bootstrap, vault operations, diagnostics, manual SSH recovery, and live lifecycle execution distinct. Never request, print, or expose secrets.
- Preserve useful targeted developer feedback; `./validate.sh` alone is not sufficient during iteration.
- Issue #187 and PR #188 establish the current validation boundary and are context, not decisions to reopen.
- Prefer the smallest coherent command set. Do not create one wrapper per raw command without a domain reason.

Working language:

- **Bash command**: a supported top-level script such as `./run.sh`.
- **Operation**: the job a command performs, such as non-live validation or inventory inspection.
- **Raw command**: a direct `uv run --locked ...` invocation shown to a human or agent.
- **Internal call**: a tool invocation inside a script or isolated test rather than part of the supported command vocabulary.
- **Non-live boundary**: contacts no managed host and uses no vault secret or machine-specific credential. It does not mean offline; public-network reads are permitted.
- **Read-only live operation**: contacts a managed host but changes no state on it. It takes the shared lifecycle lock; a mutating operation takes the exclusive lock.
- **Masked value**: a vault-derived value rendered with letters as `a`, digits as `9`, every other character literal, and whitespace as a visible token. A masked value is not a secret.

## Decisions so far

- [Inventory every documented and internal tool invocation](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/190#issuecomment-5390047817) — Reproduced the 36-line/25-shape guidance baseline and catalogued the broader script, runtime, test, live-access, sensitive-output, and existing-owner facts at commit `7ce6145`.

- [Define the supported Bash command vocabulary and ownership boundaries](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/191#issuecomment-5390175485) — Chose six purpose-named command families with one shared validated grammar, explicit ownership boundaries, serialized live execution, and a strict rule for adding commands.


- [Decide raw-command escape hatches and exception governance](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/192#issuecomment-5390409355) — Kept Bash commands as the default, allowed bounded task-scoped and standing raw-command permissions with separate agent safety decisions, and preserved explicitly requested read-only SSH diagnosis without creating new artifact rules.

- [Design setup, bootstrap, and vault command paths](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/193#issuecomment-5390504307) — Separated guided setup, targeted local reconciliation, transactional vault operations, non-disclosing agent key transfers, and live credential inspection with exact safety and migration dispositions.

- [Design targeted non-live feedback and domain-tool command paths](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/195#issuecomment-5415613826) — Made targeted lint, lifecycle-regression, test, and stack-policy feedback explicit `./validate.sh` operations, defined the non-live boundary as no-managed-host rather than offline, kept the Renovate adapter a maintainer-only raw command under a recorded standing permission, and removed every superseded raw form.

- [Design managed-host diagnostics, inventory, and recovery command paths](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/194#issuecomment-5417060476) — Split the lifecycle lock into shared read-only and exclusive mutating classes, defined `./run.sh`'s option grammar, gave `./inspect.sh` five operations and `./recover.sh` one, replaced secret-dumping inventory reads with a character-class masked value, split the prerequisite file into three layers to satisfy ADR-0002, and recorded four standing permissions.

- [Decide internal uv execution and isolated-test boundaries](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/196#issuecomment-5417640791) — Gave the live path one sourced Bash library, left the non-live commands calling `uv` directly, moved non-live-boundary enforcement into `./validate.sh` itself after measuring that 34 of 34 tests pass under a fixture inventory, deleted the script-internal whole-vault decryption, and replaced the permitted-internal-call list with a rule plus a derived live-playbook regression.

- [Define command-policy enforcement and repository migration](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/197#issuecomment-5417970975) — Put enforcement in nine `./validate.sh`-reachable tests (adding masked-value and vault non-disclosure coverage), made the guidance text check forbid superseded `./run.sh` option forms with its allowlist keyed to the five standing permissions, moved the full policy into a new `docs/command-policy.md` and replaced the now-wrong `uv run --locked` non-negotiable, deleted the two legacy vault scripts outright, and fixed four ordering constraints plus a third ADR for the lock split.

- [Synthesize the implementation-ready command disposition and CLI contract](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/198#issuecomment-5418235197) — Consolidated the full disposition matrix, command contracts, safety invariants, nine enforcement tests, migration surface, and eight-change implementation order; found the migration surface was 23 files rather than 11, replaced the forbidden-option list with a rule, widened the text check to shell `echo`/`printf`, corrected the liveness derivation to catch `delegate_to`, kept exit `75` for lock contention, and derived the mask's vault set from `ansible-inventory`'s own output.

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

_Empty._ The map is complete. #198 consolidated every decision into an implementation-ready disposition matrix, command contract, enforcement set, migration surface, and implementation order. Nothing remains to decide before `/to-spec` and `/to-tickets`.

## Out of scope

- Implementing, renaming, or removing production scripts, documentation, tests, playbooks, or skills during this map.
- Weakening `./run.sh` locking or lifecycle-wrapper enforcement.
- Making `./validate.sh` contact managed hosts.
- Redesigning Ansible-native LXC lifecycle policy.
- Standing up continuous integration ([ruled out by #197](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/197#issuecomment-5417970975)) — #196's fixture inventory and fixture passphrase remove the blocker that made it impossible, so it becomes a cheap follow-up, but building it inside this migration mixes two changes. Tracked separately.
- The `stacks/servarr/beets-flask/README.md` SSH runbook ([ruled out by #194](https://github.com/faviann/homelab-iac/issues/194#issuecomment-5417060476)) — its commands operate on media-library data inside a container, which Ansible holds no desired state for, so it is a stack runbook rather than the controller command interface.

## Question

Does the complete resolved design give every inventoried public raw command and every audited internal invocation an unambiguous outcome, with no architectural choice left for `/to-spec` or `/to-tickets`?

Produce and review the final disposition matrix: current invocation, operation, audience, managed-host effect, future Bash command and exact argument form, approved low-level escape hatch with governance, internal-call justification, or removal. Consolidate the command contracts, safety invariants, targeted feedback paths, enforcement requirements, documentation and skill migrations, implementation order, and any required ADRs. Identify and resolve gaps rather than making implementation tickets choose among alternatives.

sources.body:
## Resolution

The design is implementation-ready. Every inventoried public raw command and every audited internal invocation has one outcome, and no architectural choice is left for `/to-spec` or `/to-tickets`.

Verifying the resolved design against the tree at `7ce6145` found **seven gaps**. Four were decided here, three were slips corrected in place. The largest is that #197's migration surface is materially incomplete: a full sweep for the superseded forms finds **12 tracked files it never lists, carrying 16 sites** — and #197's own test 6 forbids those forms, so the migration and its enforcement currently disagree.

---

## 1. Gaps resolved by this ticket

### 1.1 The migration surface is 23 files, not 11

Files absent from #197's table:

| File | Superseded form | Sites |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `stacks/auth/auth/README.md` | `./run.sh --limit <h> -e stack_filter=<s>` | 1 |
| `stacks/portal/traefik3/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/public/music/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/public/readmeabook/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/public/romm/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/public/storyteller/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/seedbox/bittorrent/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/seedbox/sabnzbd/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/servarr/notifiarr/README.md` | same | 1 |
| `stacks/servarr/beets-flask/README.md` lines 149/155/161 | same — beyond the two test forms #197 lists | 3 |
| `docs/workstation-persistent-state.md` | `-e proxmox_skip_self=false` ×3, `-e lxc_base_system_reboot_enabled=false` ×1 | 4 |
| `requirements/roles.yml:3` | `ansible-galaxy role install -r requirements/roles.yml -p .ansible/roles` | 1 |
| `.agents/skills/rename-stack/SKILL.md:94` | `-e stack_filter=` quoted **to warn against it** | 1 |

**All 12 migrate inside this map's implementation.** The per-stack deploy line becomes `./run.sh --limit <host> --stack <stack>`; `docs/workstation-persistent-state.md` becomes `--include-controller` plus `-- -e lxc_base_system_reboot_enabled=false`; `requirements/roles.yml`'s install comment points at `./setup.sh bootstrap`; `rename-stack/SKILL.md:94` is handled by 1.3 below.

Allowlisting the stack READMEs instead was rejected. A contributor writing a new stack copies a neighbouring README, so an allowlist there propagates the dead form indefinitely — and `-e stack_filter=` is the single most-copied command shape in the repository. Leaving `-e stack_filter=` working contradicts #194, which made `--stack` a named option precisely because a bare `-e` is how a target filter gets defeated by accident.

### 1.2 The guidance text check sees text a shell script *prints*

#197 excluded shell scripts wholesale — "their `uv` calls are execution, not instruction." That is right for execution lines and wrong for echoed guidance. `setup.sh:288` and `configure-vault.sh:138` both print `./run.sh --tags validation` today; `rotate-vault-passphrase.sh:145` prints `ansible-vault view $VAULT_FILE`. The latter two die with their scripts, but `setup.sh` survives — and #197 itself lists "`setup.sh` echoed follow-ups" as a migration item that the check it designed cannot cover.

**The check's scope gains string literals inside `echo`/`printf` in tracked `*.sh`. Execution lines stay excluded.** This is the argument #197 already accepted for YAML `msg:` text: a message printed at the moment of failure is the most-copied guidance in the repository. Excluding `*.sh` while including `msg:` drew the seam at the file extension rather than at the distinction that matters.

The `#196` seam is unchanged and still clean: test 6 covers text that *teaches* (Markdown, YAML comments and `msg:`, and now shell `echo`/`printf` literals); `#196`'s internal-call rule plus test 4 covers text that *executes*.

### 1.3 Prose that quotes a superseded form in order to forbid it

`rename-stack/SKILL.md:94` warns that "`-e stack_filter=` short-circuits `stale` handling" — correct guidance that necessarily names the dead form. `docs/command-policy.md` and two of the three ADRs will do the same. #197 assumed shape-scoping kept such prose safe; it does not, because the prose contains the exact shape.

**The allowlist gains three entries**: `docs/command-policy.md` and `docs/adr/*.md` may name any superseded form; `.agents/skills/rename-stack/SKILL.md` gains line 94's shape alongside its permission-3 entry.

Rewriting the prose to describe rather than quote was rejected — it weakens the warning exactly where precision matters, since a reader searching for the string they just typed should find it. Exempting prose outside code fences was rejected because backticks are how the form is written in a warning *and* in an instruction, so the fence is not the signal.

### 1.4 The forbidden option forms are a rule, not a list

#197 pinned four superseded forms. The sweep found two more: `--tags provision` (`README.md:207`) and `-e lxc_base_system_reboot_enabled=false` (`docs/workstation-persistent-state.md:248`), the latter a legitimate variable that under #194's grammar must move behind `--`.

**The check enforces a rule: in a documented `./run.sh` invocation, `-e` and `--tags` may appear only after `--`.** The replacement table is kept as the *fix* guidance, not as the check's definition:

| Superseded form | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| `-e stack_filter=<stack>` | `--stack <stack>` |
| `-e proxmox_skip_self=false` | `--include-controller` |

#196 states: "a playbook is live when any play targets something other than `localhost`." The full survey supports the second clause being sufficient: `delegate_to` appears 80 times in `playbooks/`, 43 to `localhost` and 37 to Proxmox-host or Proxmox-API delegates that are reachable only from plays already targeting `lxcs` or `proxmox_api`. The one case the first clause misses is exactly L3.

Chasing `delegate_to` through role includes statically was rejected as brittle against `include_role`; a hand-pinned list is what #196 rejected.

**Recorded boundary**: a future localhost-only playbook that delegates to the Proxmox host *without* importing L3 goes undetected. Acceptable — L3 is what establishes that SSH access, so such a playbook would not work anyway.

**Consequence**: `bootstrap.yml` stops being a named exception. It is `hosts: localhost`, `connection: local`, imports no L3, and is non-live under either clause, so naming it was a no-op. The exception list is `controller-prerequisites.yml` alone.

### 1.6 Lock contention keeps exit status 75

`run.sh:26` exits **75** when it cannot take the lock. #193 standardised `0` success / `1` failed check or operation / `2` invalid usage, and no ticket reconciled the two.

**The convention is `0` / `1` / `2` / `75`, where `75` means "another holder has the lock" and is returned by `./run.sh`, `./inspect.sh`, and `./recover.sh`.** #194 deliberately chose to stop rather than wait, and that choice only pays off if the caller can distinguish "someone else is deploying" from "the deploy failed". It also preserves existing behaviour, and `75` is `EX_TEMPFAIL`, which is what this is.

`./inspect.sh vars` never returns `75` — it takes no lock.

### 1.7 `./inspect.sh vars` derives the vault set from its own output

#194's mask needs the decrypted vault key/value set for both detection rules, but #196 deleted the repository's only script-internal whole-vault decryption and #194's scope tripwire caps `vars` at one mask function plus one pass over an existing command's output.

**The set is derived from the `ansible-inventory` output itself: every merged variable named `vault_*` is a vault key, and its value is a vault value for rule 2.** `group_vars/all/vault.yml` applies to every host, so all 40 keys are already present in the output — that is *why* it leaks 73 lines. No second decryption, no second input, tripwire intact.

Cost: rule 1 becomes "named `vault_*`" rather than "a key in the vault". So the prefix stops being a convention and becomes a stated contract in `inventory/group_vars/all/vault.yml.example`, and **test 8 asserts that every key in that file carries the prefix**. All 40 tracked keys conform today.

**Recorded boundary** (in addition to #194's two): a vault key added without the `vault_` prefix is not masked by rule 1. Test 8 is what makes that a loud failure.

## 4. The command vocabulary

Six purpose-named commands. Grammar: `./command.sh [operation] [supported options] [-- low-level arguments]`. Every command documents `--help`, validates its own arguments, and rejects unknown input. `./run.sh`, `./validate.sh`, and `./setup.sh` have safe no-argument defaults. `./vault.sh`, `./inspect.sh`, and `./recover.sh` require an explicit operation. ## 5. Safety invariants

1. No supported operation prints decrypted vault contents or a secret value. Enforced by test 9.
2. `./inspect.sh vars` prints **masked values** only: letters → `a`, digits → `9`, every other character literal, whitespace as a visible token (`·`, `\n`, `\t`), runs over 16 identical mask characters collapsed to a count. Case is not preserved. Enforced by test 8.
3. Vault plaintext exists only inside a mode-700 tmpfs workspace, never at the tracked vault path. Mutations validate and encrypt before atomically replacing `inventory/group_vars/all/vault.yml`; failure leaves the original untouched. Retained backups are ciphertext, mode 600, outside the repository.
4. Every operation that contacts a managed host goes through the single live-execution path: wrapper marker, locked `uv`, target selection, declared prerequisite layers.
5. Read-only live operations take a shared lock; mutating ones take an exclusive lock; non-live operations take none. A command that cannot take its lock **stops immediately** with exit `75` and names the holder. There is no `--wait`.
6. `./validate.sh` contacts no managed host, uses no vault secret, and uses no machine-specific credential. It does **not** promise offline execution — public-network reads are permitted and documented as such.
7. An agent must not read or print secrets. A masked value produced by `./inspect.sh vars` is not a secret. This exemption is scoped to that one command with that one documented mask.
8. A human-approved raw command is not automatically agent-safe. Silence means human-only, and an agent cannot approve its own exception.
9. `./recover.sh ssh-keys` keeps ADR-0002's minimal identity validation — vmid, hostname, resolved control-node public key — and never runs LXC contract compilation or fleet preflight.

## 9. ADRs

Three, each landing with its change:

1. **The masked value** (change 7) — an agent may print a derivative of a secret; argued both ways (closed flag list versus open mask, case preserved versus collapsed); hard to reverse once masked output has reached transcripts and pull requests. It also amends a security rule set by #192.
2. **Enforcing the non-live boundary in the validation command** (change 4) — a validation command silently overrides Ansible's inventory and vault password, and nothing in the 39 test files shows it.
3. **The shared/exclusive lock split** (change 3) — surprising that a read-only command takes a lock at all; a real trade-off (`--wait` rejected, check mode audited rather than trusted); hard to reverse once `inspect.sh` and `recover.sh` depend on it. It amends ADR-0001's linear-execution model and should be findable beside it.
